title: Evaluating a new high‑dose aflibercept injection for people with polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy that has not responded well to standard care
official: Evaluating a new high‑dose aflibercept injection for people with polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy that has not responded well to standard care
summary:
Background and study aims
Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (PCV) is a type of wet age-related macular degeneration that can cause fluid, bleeding, and swelling at the back of the eye, leading to blurred or distorted vision. Many people with PCV need frequent anti-VEGF eye injections to keep the condition under control. Some patients continue to have active disease despite regular treatment. Aflibercept 8 mg (Eylea 8mg) is a newer, higher-dose version of an established treatment for macular disease. It is also an approved and available treatment for wet age-related macular degeneration. Early studies suggest that the higher dose may control PCV more effectively and may reduce the need for very frequent injections. However, its benefit specifically in patients whose PCV remains active on standard treatment is not yet fully understood. The PROSPER8 study aims to find out how well aflibercept 8 mg works in people with treatment-resistant PCV.

Who can participate?
Patients with PCV affecting the central part of their vision, identified on an diagnostic scan by enlarged choroidal vessels, a raised or unusually shaped area under the retina, and fluid beneath the retina, and they are currently being treated with standard antiVEGF injections (not the 8 mg dose of aflibercept) that need to be given every 8 weeks or more often, who are at Moorfields Eye Hospital.

What does the study involve?
Everyone in the study will receive aflibercept 8 mg injections at the start of the study and again at 4 and 8 weeks. They will then be reviewed at 16 and 24 weeks. At each visit, participants will have eye examinations and scans to check whether the PCV has become inactive, whether vision has improved or stabilised, and whether swelling under the retina has reduced. The study will also look at detailed imaging features to understand which patients respond best.

What are the possible benefits of participating?
Aflibercept 8 mg is already licensed and routinely used in the NHS for macular disease, so all treatments and tests in this study are part of standard eye care. Taking part is voluntary, and participants can withdraw at any time without affecting their usual treatment. The results of this study will help doctors understand whether aflibercept 8 mg offers better
control of PCV in patients who continue to have active disease on their current injections. This may guide future treatment decisions and improve outcomes for people living with this condition.

What are the possible risks of participating?
Participants will receive aflibercept 8 mg, a treatment already in routine NHS use, and the risks are similar to standard intravitreal injections. Common side effects (up to 1 in 10 people) include eye soreness, a temporary rise in eye pressure, small surface bleeds on the eye, and floaters. Rare complications (up to 1 in 1000 people) include infection inside the eye, retinal detachment, cataract, bleeding within the eye, or severe inflammation, which can lead to reduced vision if not treated promptly. Vision may be blurred for several hours after the injection, and participants should not drive on the day of treatment. As with all anti-VEGF therapies, aflibercept may pose a risk to pregnancy; therefore, pregnancy is an exclusion criterion and effective contraception is required until 3 months after the final dose. Fluorescein dye used for angiography may cause nausea or flushing, and severe allergic reactions are very rare. 

Where is the study run from?
Moorfields Eye Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
October 2026 to October 2027.

Who is funding the study?
Bayer, UK.

Who is the main contact?
Dr Luke Nicholson, Moorfields Eye Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, luke.nicholson3@nhs.net

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Age 45 or above 
2. Capacity to consent to treatment and participation in trial 
3. Signed informed consent 
4. Diagnosis of active polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy involving the fovea with the greatest linear dimension of <5400µm – diagnosis is investigator dependent based on OCT. OCT criteria for diagnosis of PCV are 1) presence of pachychoroid vessels 2) peaked or notched or multilobulated pigment epithelial detachment AND 3) subretinal fluid 
5. On active treatment with anti-VEGF monotherapy (excluding Aflibercept 8mg) requiring treatment intervals of 8 weeks or less  
6. Best corrected visual acuity of 78 letters to 24 ETDRS letters 
7. Women of child-bearing potential and men, when sexually active, must agree to use adequate contraception from the time point of signing the informed consent form until 3 months after the last study drug administration. Acceptable methods of contraception include (1) condoms (male or female) (2) diaphragm or cervical cap with spermicide; (3) intra-uterine device; (4) hormone-based contraception
Exclusion criteria:
1. Any ocular disorders in the study eye that, in the opinion of the investigator, may impact interpretation of study results or interfere with subject safety, including; 
1.1. Visually significant media opacities including cataract 
1.2. Decrease in BCVA due to causes other than wet AMD/PCV 
1.3. History or presence of diabetic macular oedema or more than mild nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy, vitreomacular traction or epiretinal membrane causing retinal thickening in the study eye  
1.4. Previous adverse reaction to aflibercept 8mg 
1.5. Active ocular inflammation or external ocular inflammation in the study eye  
1.6. Pregnant
